article.title: A shocking Iowa poll means somebody is going to be wrong
article.subtitle: Either Ann Selzer and the New York Times, or the rest of the polling industry.

extraction.summary: Silver analyzes the November 2024 Selzer/Des Moines Register Iowa poll showing Harris +3 (47-44). He argues it is probably wrong given priors and Iowa's 2020 Trump +8 result, but it is informative. In the Silver Bulletin model it raised Harris's Iowa win probability from 9% to 17%. It left her overall odds roughly unchanged, because Iowa has only a 1% tipping-point chance and is highly correlated with the Blue Wall states, especially Wisconsin. The article shows a 40,000-simulation state correlation matrix, conditional outcomes given a Harris Iowa win, and the model's use of county-based regions. Silver also discusses herding in heavily polled swing states, a possible inflation-based geographic pattern in 2020-to-2024 shifts, and a list of polling anomalies that raise his concern about a systematic polling error of unknown direction.

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings as of November 2024, Selzer & Co. and NYT/Siena College are the two highest-rated pollsters.
findings.rationale: Both have long track records of bucking conventional wisdom and being right.
findings.evidence_quote: Selzer and NYT/Siena are our two highest-rated pollsters.

findings.statement: In the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model, the Selzer Iowa poll (Harris +3) raised Harris's chance of winning Iowa from 9% to 17%. A single high-quality poll in a sparsely polled state can nearly double a state win probability.

quantities.name: Harris Iowa win probability before Selzer poll
Harris Iowa win probability after Selzer poll
Selzer poll result
quantities.context: Final Selzer/Des Moines Register Iowa poll, 2024

findings.evidence_quote: Harris's chances of winning Iowa nearly doubled in our model from 9 percent to 17 percent tonight

findings.statement: Polymarket's Harris-wins-Iowa price moved similarly to the Silver Bulletin model after the Selzer poll, rising from 6% to 18%.
findings.evidence_quote: Polymarket shows a similar trend, moving from 6 percent to 18 percent after the survey.

findings.statement: The margin of error on the lead (the difference between candidates) in a poll is roughly double the reported per-candidate margin of error. For an 808-likely-voter poll, the 95% margin of error on the margin is ±6.6 points.

quantities.name: Margin of error on the lead

findings.evidence_quote: the margin of error for the difference separating the candidates in a poll of that size is ±6.6 points.

findings.statement: Theoretical sampling margins of error understate true polling error. They do not capture non-sampling sources, especially nonresponse: the overwhelming majority of people pollsters try to contact never complete the survey.
findings.rationale: Nonresponse bias adds error beyond sampling error.
findings.evidence_quote: The theory, however, doesn't capture all possible sources of polling error — especially the fact that the overwhelming majority of people who pollsters attempt to contact never complete the survey.

findings.statement: A forecaster should be Bayesian and combine a surprising poll with priors such as the state's previous result. Flipping a state lost by 8 points last time is a big ask, so a single poll showing it should be discounted.
findings.evidence_quote: we ought to be good Bayesians here: even if Harris has a very good night on Tuesday, winning a state you lost last time by 8 points is a big ask.

findings.statement: Silver describes Emerson College as a firm that herds heavily, virtually never publishing results that defy conventional wisdom, and says readers should account for that when interpreting its polls. Its final 2024 Iowa poll was Trump +9, with a 95% interval of Trump +15.7 to Trump +2.5.
findings.rationale: Herding makes a poll less independent and less informative.
findings.evidence_quote: Emerson is a firm that does a lot of herding, so you ought to account for that — they virtually never publish a survey that defies the conventional wisdom.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin Iowa polling average stood at Trump +3.4 after the Selzer poll, but rested on only 4 Iowa polls all cycle, so it carries substantial uncertainty.
findings.evidence_quote: our current polling average in Iowa falls just within that range of overlap: Trump +3.4 points. (Careful: the "average" is based on only 4 polls of Iowa all cycle long.)

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin state polling averages account for each poll's quality, sample size and recency. They are also adjusted using trends in both state and national polls, so a state average can move even without new state polls.

The Silver Bulletin Iowa polling average chart shows Trump 48.8% and Harris 45.4% on Nov 2, 2024. The average starts in mid-September and moves in visible steps when new polls arrive (one jump around Oct 1, one at the end of October), which reflects sparse state polling.

In the 2024 Silver Bulletin model, a big Iowa poll barely moved the national forecast. Iowa had only a 1% chance of being the tipping-point state, because its outcomes are highly correlated with the Blue Wall states, especially Wisconsin. By the time Harris wins Iowa she has usually already won the Blue Wall.
findings.rationale: Correlated states are redundant for Electoral College paths.
findings.evidence_quote: mostly it's because Iowa is unlikely — only a 1 percent chance — to be the tipping-point state. The reason is that its outcomes are likely to be highly correlated with the Blue Wall states

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 model's simulated state outcome correlations (from 40,000 simulations) for Iowa are: Iowa-Wisconsin .84, Iowa-Michigan .70, Iowa-Pennsylvania .69, Iowa-North Carolina .57, Iowa-Arizona .48, Iowa-Nevada .35, Iowa-Georgia .31.

Simulated correlations among the 2024 swing states in the Silver Bulletin model are: MI-PA .82, MI-WI .83, PA-WI .81, GA-NC .82, AZ-NV .82, MI-GA .57, MI-NC .72, MI-AZ .63, MI-NV .56, PA-GA .55, PA-NC .73, PA-AZ .65, PA-NV .52, WI-GA .41, WI-NC .65, WI-AZ .60, WI-NV .49, GA-AZ .48, GA-NV .40, NC-AZ .60, NC-NV .44. Regional blocs (Blue Wall, Sun Belt South, Southwest) are the most tightly correlated.
The 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast runs 40,000 simulations per model run.
findings.evidence_quote: In our 40,000 simulations tonight

findings.statement: In 2024 Silver Bulletin simulations where Harris won Iowa, her average margin was +6.7 in Wisconsin, +5.9 in Michigan and +3.8 in Pennsylvania. Conditional on winning Iowa, she won Wisconsin 98% of the time.

quantities.name: Avg WI margin given Harris wins IA
Avg MI margin given Harris wins IA
Avg PA margin given Harris wins IA

findings.evidence_quote: Conditional on winning Iowa, her chances in Wisconsin are 98 percent, for instance.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin model defines geographic regions by county rather than by state, so more than a dozen states straddle two or more regions. About two-thirds of Pennsylvania's population falls in the Northeast region rather than the Midwest, which makes Pennsylvania less correlated with Iowa than Wisconsin or Michigan are.

quantities.name: Share of PA population in Northeast region

findings.rationale: County-level regions capture within-state heterogeneity in correlation structure.
findings.evidence_quote: about two-thirds of its population is in what we consider the Northeast, not the Midwest like Iowa. (Our regions are divided by county, not state — so more than a dozen states straddle two or more of them.)

findings.statement: In the 2024 Silver Bulletin simulations, scenarios where Iowa is decisive are rare. Examples: Harris loses Pennsylvania but wins Iowa plus North Carolina (273-265). Harris wins the Blue Wall plus Iowa but loses New Hampshire (271-267 rather than 267). Harris loses New Mexico, offset by Iowa (271-267). Weird far-tail maps also occur where polling is a disaster but the Electoral College lands near 269-269.
findings.evidence_quote: The most plausible case probably involves North Carolina, but it's still quite rare in our simulations

findings.statement: The 2024 Silver Bulletin model projected Harris to win New Mexico by about 7 points on average, yet gave Trump an 11% chance there. The model is more uncertain about eccentric, sparsely polled states, and weak Harris polling in nearby Arizona and Nevada feeds into New Mexico through regional correlation.
findings.rationale: Little polling means wider uncertainty, and regional correlation transmits signal from neighboring states.
findings.evidence_quote: it's also pretty uncertain about an eccentric state without much polling. And Harris's polling has been weak in nearby Arizona and Nevada, so it does have Trump winning it 11 percent of the time.

findings.statement: Silver theorizes that pollsters herd heavily in high-profile swing states (WI, MI, PA) while showing their true numbers in more obscure Midwestern states. The 2024 Silver Bulletin model is not sophisticated enough to account for differential herding by state profile. Silver says readers should infer that Harris might outperform her Blue Wall polls, especially in Wisconsin.
findings.evidence_quote: Our model isn't quite sophisticated enough to go into this level of detail

findings.statement: Fewer than 10% of 2024 polls in states like Wisconsin showed anything outside Harris +2 to Trump +2. Sampling error alone makes that statistically very unlikely, which is evidence of herding.
findings.evidence_quote: Why so few polls in states like Wisconsin — less than 10 percent! — dare to show anything outside the range of Harris +2 to Trump +2

findings.statement: Silver lists anomalies in 2024 polling that raise his concern about a systematic polling error of unknown direction. Likely-voter models help Harris nationally but hurt her in swing states. Non-herding pollsters (Selzer, NYT/Siena) differ sharply from the rest. Large crosstab shifts among Black and Latino voters produce small topline swings. Swing-state polls are too tightly clustered. A favorability gap favors Harris but she does not consistently lead head-to-heads. National polls moved toward Trump more than battleground polls did.
findings.rationale: Herding may concentrate on head-to-heads, which pollsters tinker with more than favorability ratings.
findings.evidence_quote: I've become increasingly concerned about the possibility of another systematic polling error — although I don't know whether it will favor Trump, favor Harris, or produce a map that's just really strange.

findings.statement: On Nov 2, 2024, the final round of AtlasIntel polls (a highly rated pollster with bearish numbers for Harris) entered the Silver Bulletin database just before the model run. These polls offset what might otherwise have been a decent update toward Harris. Silver says the model should in future (2026/2028) show which surveys are new since the last update.
findings.rationale: Transparency about which new polls drive each update.
findings.evidence_quote: Absent those, the model might have updated a decent amount to Harris.

findings.statement: Silver reports a statistically significant correlation between state-level inflation since Biden took office and the 2020-to-2024 shifts shown in polls. Harris held up in the low-inflation Midwest (except high-inflation Minnesota) and in North Carolina, but lost ground in high-inflation Florida, Nevada, Arizona, New York and Virginia. This geographic inflation effect is not described as a model input.
findings.rationale: Possible mechanism for regionally varying swings.
findings.evidence_quote: this is conspicuously (and statistically significantly!) well-correlated with where the polls have shown shifts from 2020.

findings.statement: As of Nov 2, 2024 the Silver Bulletin forecast was almost exactly 50/50, a true toss-up rather than tilting Trump. Silver said any October Trump momentum had petered out, and that final high-quality polls split roughly evenly between implying a Harris win and implying a Trump win.
findings.evidence_quote: the election is now almost truly back to being 50/50.

political_insights.insight: Iowa trended strongly red through 2020 (Trump +8). Selzer polls in 2024 swung from Trump +18 versus Biden in June to Trump +4 versus Harris in September to Harris +3 in November.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Large candidate-switch effects are possible. Treat single-pollster series in sparse states carefully.

political_insights.insight: Harris held up in the Midwest (except Minnesota), NE-02 and Ohio, and lost ground in Florida, the Southwest (NV, AZ), New York and Virginia, which may be tied to state-level inflation.
political_insights.evidence: NE-02 average Harris +9.6 vs Biden's 6.6 in 2020; Ohio poll Harris -3; a tight Kansas poll; inflation regression
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Regional, not uniform, swing structure; consider state-level economic conditions.

political_insights.insight: Crosstabs show Harris losing ground with Black and Latino voters, but toplines move little. These shifts may be real and even larger than published polls show.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Sun Belt states with large minority populations may carry correlated error.

political_insights.insight: Harris had underwhelming margins in Minnesota despite Tim Walz being her running mate.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: The VP home-state effect may be small.

open_questions: The full functional form generating state correlations, including how county-based regions enter the correlation structure.
How the polling average adjusts for state and national trends when a state has few polls.
Whether and how the model penalizes herding pollsters such as Emerson.
How much weight a single top-rated poll receives in a sparse-poll state.
